content: 1. Embedded systems are integrated into various functions and processes. 2. A healthy diet consists of a balanced, diverse, and appropriate selection of foods consumed over time. 3. A healthy diet ensures that the requirements for macronutrients (proteins, fats, carbohydrates, including dietary fibers) and essential micronutrients (vitamins, minerals, and trace elements) are met, tailored to an individual’s gender, age, physical activity level, and physiological state. 4. To maintain a healthy diet: Daily energy, vitamin, and mineral needs must be met without exceeding energy requirements. Consumption of fruits and vegetables should exceed 400 grams per day. Saturated fat intake should be less than 10% of total energy intake. Trans-fat intake should be less than 1% of total energy intake. Free sugar intake should be less than 10% of total energy intake, ideally below 5%. Salt intake should be less than 5 grams per day. 5. For infants and young children, a healthy diet is similar to that of adults but includes additional considerations: Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the first six months of life. Breastfeeding should continue up to two years of age and beyond. From six months of age, breast milk should be complemented with a variety of safe, nutrient-dense foods. Salt and sugars should not be added to complementary foods. 6. Hunger is defined as an uncomfortable or painful physical sensation caused by insufficient dietary energy consumption. In this context, hunger is synonymous with chronic undernourishment. 7. Malnutrition refers to an abnormal physiological condition caused by inadequate, unbalanced, or excessive consumption of macronutrients and/or micronutrients. It includes undernutrition (child stunting, wasting, and vitamin/mineral deficiencies) as well as overweight and obesity. 8. Micronutrients are vitamins, minerals, and other substances required by the body in small amounts, measured in milligrams or micrograms. 9. The multiple burdens of malnutrition refer to the coexistence of undernutrition (stunting, wasting, and micronutrient deficiencies) alongside overweight and obesity within the same country, community, household, or individual. 10. Nutrition security exists when secure access to an appropriately nutritious diet is coupled with a sanitary environment, adequate health services, and care, ensuring a healthy and active life for all household members. It differs from food security by also considering caregiving practices, health, and hygiene. 11. Nutrition-sensitive interventions address the underlying determinants of nutrition, such as household food security, maternal and child care, primary healthcare, and sanitation, without necessarily having nutrition as the primary goal. 12. Nutritional status is the physiological state of an individual resulting from the relationship between nutrient intake and requirements, as well as the body’s ability to digest, absorb, and utilize these nutrients. 13. Overweight and obesity are defined as body weight above normal for height due to excessive fat accumulation. In adults, overweight is defined as a BMI of 25 kg/m² or more, and obesity as a BMI of 30 kg/m² or more. In children under five, overweight is defined as weight-for-height greater than two standard deviations above the WHO Child Growth Standards median, and obesity as greater than three standard deviations above the median. 14. Processed foods are industrially manufactured products where salt, sugar, or other culinary ingredients are added to unprocessed or minimally processed foods to preserve them or enhance their palatability. These products often contain two or three ingredients and may involve cooking or fermentation processes. Additives may be used to maintain product properties or prevent microbial growth. 15. Ultra-processed food products are industrial formulations with multiple ingredients, including culinary substances like fats, oils, salt, and sugar, as well as additives to modify color, flavor, taste, or texture. Examples include soft drinks, packaged snacks, instant noodles, and chicken nuggets. 16. Stunting refers to low height-for-age, reflecting past episodes of sustained undernutrition. In children under five, stunting is defined as height-for-age less than two standard deviations below the WHO Child Growth Standards median. 17. Wasting refers to low weight-for-height, often resulting from recent inadequate dietary energy intake or disease. In children under five, wasting is defined as weight-for-height less than two standard deviations below the WHO Child Growth Standards median. 18. Sustainable use involves utilizing components of biological diversity in a way and at a rate that does not lead to long-term decline, ensuring its potential to meet the needs and aspirations of present and future generations. 19. Resilience is the capacity of an ecosystem or society to withstand disturbances without crossing a threshold into a different structure or output. It depends on ecological dynamics and the organizational and institutional capacity to understand, manage, and respond to these dynamics. 20. Stakeholder consultations aim to understand baseline conditions that may inhibit or facilitate progress toward mainstreaming biodiversity for health and nutrition co-benefits. This involves identifying threats, raising awareness, and empowering local stakeholders to engage in the process. 21. Indicators are scored on a five-point scale to assess baseline status and trends in biodiversity management and diet-related health outcomes. Group discussions and scoring help identify common perceptions, threats, and solutions. 22. Preliminary actions for mainstreaming biodiversity into local and national plans are identified based on scoring results, emphasizing community ownership and collaboration. 23. Following consultations, outcomes are analyzed to produce reports with results, entry points for mainstreaming, and potential next steps for pilot phases.
